did_you_know.text: Did you know? The cities of refuge were not established solely on human initiative: the Lord commanded Joshua to establish them, just as the Israelites had previously been commanded to do so in the days of Moses.
Did you know? The purpose of the cities of refuge was to protect someone who had unintentionally killed another person—that is, without intent or prior hostility—from the avenger of blood.

Did you know? The fugitive did not enter the city automatically: he had to stand at the city gate, explain what had happened to the city elders, and only then would they take him in and give him a place to live.

Did you know? The verse explicitly distinguishes between accidental killing and killing motivated by hatred: if the person had not hated the victim, he would not be handed over to the avenger of blood before the case was investigated.

Did you know? The fugitive remained in the city of refuge until he stood trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest serving at that time; afterward, he was permitted to return to his city and his home.

Did you know? Three of the cities of refuge were in the land west of the Jordan: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Hebron—which is Kiriath-arba—in the hill country of Judah.
Did you know? The other three cities of refuge were east of the Jordan: Bezer in the territory of Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead in the territory of Gad, and Golan in Bashan in the territory of Manasseh.
Did you know? The six cities of refuge were intended not only for the Israelites, but also for the foreigners living among them.

Did you know? The role of the cities of refuge was to ensure that anyone who had accidentally killed another person would not be killed by the avenger of blood before standing trial before the assembly.
